FACDEV.TITLE: Advanced Practices in Generative AI in the classroom
FACDEV.DESC:
Leaping Forward: Advanced Practices in Generative AI
Educators are catching up to the promise of AI, but it’s not always clear how to implement these tools in our individual disciplines. This workshop is for faculty who understand how to use AI but are seeking creative ideas for actual deployment in their classes. Participants will be able to preview dozens of examples before the workshop, then participate interactively during the workshop to adjust their own assignments for an AI-infused world. We’ll also tackle the thorny problem of teaching fundamentals even when the software can do everything. Finally, we will put AI to work making faculty life easier with writing syllabi, lesson plans, and other documents.

Before attending this webinar, you should already know the basics of LLMs. If needed, a one-hour primer webinar (video) is available here.

You may also want to quickly scan through our open-source book on “ChatGPT Assignments to Use in Your Classroom Today”: https://stars.library.ucf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1097&context=oer

FACDEV.TITLE: Leveraging Generative AI for Engineering Course Development: Save Yourself Time and Improve Student Learning
FACDEV.DESC: Join us for an insightful presentation that explores the transformative potential of generative AI in engineering education. This informative session will delve into how faculty can harness tools like ChatGPT, MidJourney, Gamma, custom-built GPTs, and other generative AI tools to streamline course development and elevate educational outcomes. Discover practical applications of AI for creating high-quality presentations, comprehensive lecture notes, targeted learning objectives, and robust assessments. This presentation will not only demonstrate these tools but also engage in critical discussions on the ethical use of AI in education, its environmental implications, and how to address the challenge of academic integrity in the digital age. Whether you're looking to enhance your teaching efficiency or enrich student learning experiences, this talk will equip you with the knowledge and tools to integrate AI effectively into your educational practices.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is located in the historic Texan borderlands created at the end of the Mexican-American war in 1848 which separated families on both sides of the Rio Grande River. The university was formed in 2013 when The University of Texas at Brownsville and The University of Texas Pan-American were consolidated to expand educational opportunities in the underserved and rural Valley of the Rio Grande. UTRGV is a major Hispanic-Serving Institution (HSI), primarily a nonresidential, 4-year, public, R2 institution, with campuses situated along the lower 100 miles of the Rio Grande. UTRGV's student demographics mirror those of the Lower Rio Grande Valley (RGV), with over 95% of our 32,000 students being of Hispanic or Latinx origin (Region One Education Service Center, 2021), and over 85% having Mexican-American heritage. Academic programs in engineering, started in 1992, were first accredited by ABET in 1996. The College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) currently has 6 departments offering 8 bachelors' and 7 masters' degrees. The college has over 110 faculty members and serves nearly 3900 students, mostly (90%) undergraduates. Although CECS does not have a PhD program yet, a pathway for a doctoral degree is offered jointly with the University of Nebraska at Lincoln (UNL). As the second largest HSI in the nation, UTR V is uniquely positioned to broaden the participation of Hispanics in the engineering workforce.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Freshwater Prawn Production: Solving the National Problem of Prawn Postlarvae (Seed) Availability through Engineering and Automation
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The United States imports billions of dollars of shrimp and other seafoods yearly. Farming large freshwater shrimp (i.e., prawns) can help address this deficit. However, although prawns are
successfully farmed in Asia and other parts of the world, they have failed to find success in the U.S. The most fundamental problem has been that the hatchery production of seed (i.e., small prawns) is highly technical, labor intensive, and prohibitively expensive to ship, resulting in farmers lacking access to affordable seed. This project proposes to acquire preliminary and proof of concept data for an automated, inexpensive, and simple to use larvae production system that farmers can use to produce prawn seed. The system is called LIKE (Larvae Intensive Kinetic Environment) and uses a downward-thrusting propeller to create water currents that power much of the system’s automation
and technical simplicity. Preliminary work by the Applicants has confirmed the basic principles on which the LIKE system operates, however the Applicants lacked the resources to gather the data
necessary to demonstrate that the prawn seed problem has been resolved. Seed funding is thus being sought to obtain this necessary data. These data will enable the Applicants to apply for future AFRI grants pertaining to regional hatcheries, adult prawn culture, and the sustainable development of a U.S. prawn industry, all of which have the prerequisite of demonstrating the availability of affordable prawn seed. The broader outcome of this work will be to reduce U.S. dependance on imported shrimp and providing income opportunities to U.S. farmers.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Facilitating Sustainable and Profitable Oyster Culture: Promoting Equity of Opportunities for Texas’ Lower Laguna Madre.
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The main objectives of this proposal are to: 1) Establish an oyster seed hatchery to service the LLM and its surrounding communities; 2) Develop low-cost, low maintenance oyster grow out equipment/methods suitable for the LLM; 3) Investigate the effects of these grow-out methods on seagrasses and 4) Establish a Beginning Oyster Farmer Incubator (BOFI) to provide the education and extension services necessary to ensure that oyster culture is both sustainable and assessable to all. The outcome of this proposal will both provide the oyster seed necessary to make oyster culture in the LLM possible, and reverse current inequalities and allow the Applicant’s targeted end users (socioeconomically disadvantaged/underserved communities), to also participate and benefit from oyster culture in the Lower Laguna Madre.

These objectives frame a model that is applicable not only to the LLM, but can be modified to support disadvantaged/underserved coastal communities across the nation.

CONGRANT.TITLE: NSF FM SG Cyber
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Overview: Rapid changes in technology, customer preferences, and customer choices are making a significant impact on Future Manufacturing. These fast changes are making seismic shifts in the workforce environment too. It is imperative to train our future students and workers for this dynamic shift in the manufacturing environment. It is possible only if we develop a clear understanding of the changing ecosystem of Future Manufacturing. We are witnessing many technological, demographic, and consumption changes. Industry 4.0 has destined that Future Manufacturing will be Distributed Manufacturing. COVID-19 has shown the magnitude of disruption for the Vertically Integrated Centralized Manufacturing (VICM), perpetuated by the Chinese Establishment. Even if this Chinese model has given the consumers a significant cost advantage, the present pandemic has suddenly made the fault line of this model obvious and glaring in terms of uncertainty in product delivery, quality, and even product substitution. Given this unprecedented disruption, we are proposing an alternative model of Globally Balanced Distributed Manufacturing (GBDM). The proposed model will take full advantage of Industry 4.0 and offer customers guaranteed delivery on time and Quality. Intellectual Merit: We are proposing a Globally Balanced Distributed Manufacturing (GBDM) system that is digitally connected using AI-augmented Cloud service. Our model will identify customer needs using a novel platform called Edited Platform proposed by one of our Co-PIs. A digital avatar of the proposed product will be transmitted via secured Blockchain to a local manufacturer who will convert the digital art into a physical part. This will not only guarantee both Quality and deliverability, but the enterprise manufacturer can also add a local touch (product to packaging) to the product for the customer. Our model is based on AI (Artificial Intelligence) augmented Secured Cloud-Based Smart Additive Manufacturing. During COVID 19 lockdown our graduating mechanical engineering students completed their product designs at home and the teammates independently checked the design in different physical locations. Finally, our Graduate Research Assistants printed the design for demonstration in yet another physical location. This process validated the concept of Distributed Manufacturing. The customer, design engineer, manufacturer, and the business enterprise can be in several different geographical locations, yet they can communicate and manufacture the product. We are proposing to generalize this concept of AI-augmented Cloud-based Smart Additive Manufacturing for any design, simple or complex. The expertise of our Co-PIs includes Edited Platform, Network Security, and Distributed Manufacturing, among others. We plan to add a few selected AI features to improve the Quality of 3D Printed parts. We have an excellent collaborative relationship with local manufacturers to validate this model as noted by the Support Letters. Broader Impacts: To prepare our workforce for Future Manufacturing, universities have a big role to play. We need to prepare our students in relevant areas like computer skills, robotics, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Blockchain technology, network security, and Smart Manufacturing. They need to also understand the basic concepts of Globally Balanced Distributed Manufacturing, Network Security, and, of course, Smart Additive Manufacturing (SAM). We are a Minority-Serving Hispanic University with more than 30,000 students who are bi-lingual and bi-cultural. Our students are poised to take advantage of Future Manufacturing aka Industry 4.0. Local industries are excited to take advantage of this opportunity by collaborating with the University and offering our students needed training and opportunities. This Fund will both validate the concept and train our students for many jobs that do not exist today. The University has an established training center for our students and local community called TMAC (Texas Manufacturing Assistance Center). This funding can fully leverage that program with a relatively modest investment.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Design and Development: Transforming Underrepresented Minority Students Into Regional and National Engineering Innovators
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: We propose a first program in a sequence that will address these issues. The focus of the proposed program will be on the development of critical non-technical skills on high school-to-freshman students as other programs already exist to address technical skills. The proposed intervention will promote the development of technical and non-technical skills through innovation experiences that aim to not only teach the principles of the innovation process, but also teach students how to transform themselves by applying said innovation principles. Engineering students collect a cumulus of STEM knowledge trusting and assuming that it will eventually become useful. It is common for engineering students to fail to connect their acquired knowledge to practical and relevant applications. Design and Innovation provides an excellent opportunity to make these connections by working on real-life regional challenges that provide a purpose to the learned knowledge and a motivation to become better students and professionals. Challenge Based Intruction (CBI) will be used as the pedagogical approach to present these innovation experiences to the students. CBI has proven to help students develop adaptive expertise, which in this case is key to not only create an innovation or learn the innovation process, but also apply innovation to self. These innovation experiences will be calibrated by first evaluating incoming high school students to identify their technical and non-technical deficiencies and re-evaluating to see how these skills are being developed after the proposed interventions. Initially it won’t be feasible to include every single incoming engineering student in the proposed program; our aim is to intervene a selected group to create a critical mass of transformed innovator students that can have an initial impact on their classroom communities. These students will lead communities of learning and take other initiatives that will help disseminate innovation thinking, serve as models and motivate other non-participating students. Future programs will focus on a sequence of increasingly complex innovation experiences through sophomore, junior and senior years aimed at developing self as a student, as a professional and as an innovator. Our overarching goal is to prepare professional engineers that can help in the development of the RGV region by generating their own opportunities for innovation.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV), a major Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI)
located in the border region of United States and Mexico is seeking to increase participation, retention
and graduation rates among minority low-income students in the critically needed engineering and
technology programs. This project provides innovative ways for adapting effective evidence based
curricular and co-curricular activities aimed to improve undergraduate student academic success. The
primary goal of this project is to encourage and increase the number of students towards obtaining their
degrees in STEM by providing 30 undergradaute students with four-year scholarships, and 17
undergraduate students with two-year scholarships (47 total), spread across four cohorts. In addition, we
emphasize on improved student technical workforce readiness levels by establishing an academic support
system at the College of Engineering and Computer Science (COECS) to encourage students to pursue
careers in emerging fields of engineering and technology.
Building on existing student support services at UTRGV, this project includes technical and academic
success workshops, professional development, peer mentoring, industry certifications and internships, and
developing course modules integrated with Engineering Technology and Manufacturing Engineering
curriculum. The objectives identified to meet the primary project goal include: (a) To increase student
enrollment of Manufacturing and Engineering Technology undergraduate programs created to train and
prepare students with high-tech skills in the fields of manufacturing, automation and systems engineering;
(b) Developing an Eco-System in COECS with tailored student centric activities to address student’s precollege
experience, social-cultural experience, institutional experience, and college experience
specifically targeting underrepresented demographics; (c) Financially support undergraduate students by
awarding S-STEM scholarships over the grant period; and (d) Build partnerships with industry to provide
more learning and internship opportunities for students.

CONGRANT.TITLE: US-Peru Study Abroad Program: Training Engineers as Resilient Innovators
CONGRANT.SPONORG: 100,000 Strong in the Americas Innovation Fund
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
How can we effectively train our students to be successful in an ever-changing world? On one hand we have great scientific and technological discoveries and on the other a growing list of challenges such as poverty, hunger, limited access to clean water, among others (UN Sustainable Goals). Our region, country and world require resilient innovators that can create opportunities as independent entrepreneurs, or as part of industry, business or a local community organization. We must train our students to become agents of change, applying their STEAM  knowledge to provide technical solutions to solve society’s problems. Design challenges can provide a motivational, engaging, comprehensive, and realistic context for students to apply their knowledge and to understand the sustainability of a solution. Sustainability in this case has a broader sense and includes not only technical feasibility, but also ethical implications, sociocultural impact, financial structure, IP  protection, and environmental impact, among other considerations. 
For this reason, we propose the US-Peru Study Abroad Program: Training Students as Resilient Innovators between the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and the Universidad Nacional de Ingenieria (UNI) in Lima, Peru. In essence this program will provide a “micro-entrepreneurship” experience with service learning projects in the Rio Grande Valley and Lima regions. Students from any college or department will be selected to work in bi-national multidisciplinary teams to develop technological products to address a regional need (e.g. access to clean water, home technologies, etc.). In the first part of the program UNI students will visit UTRGV and then UTRGV students will visit UNI. The teams will receive training and support for their specific projects in a variety of relevant topics such as engineering design, sociocultural considerations, and business modeling. This will be complemented with site visits (e.g. local industry, research centers, etc.), guest presentations (e.g. government officials, NGO representatives, etc.) and sociocultural experiences (e.g. visits to Machu Picchu, Lima’s colonial sites, etc.). At the end of the program, the students will present their solutions to a “shark tank” of academicians, community representatives and entrepreneurs. Each team must apply for a patent and also learn the process of submitting their product to a regional or national student innovation funding competition.
Our objective is to engage the UTRGV and UNI student communities by learning from each other and creating a culture of innovation where anyone can tackle a real problem and file a patent. We will train our students as resilient innovators to overcome scarcity of resources through creativity and resourcefulness. This will be achieved by providing a non-traditional learning environment outside the classroom where students apply STEAM knowledge to develop technical and professional skills by working on a real problem.
The RGV and Lima innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem is emerging and our regions face multiple similar challenges. Our regions will benefit from these resilient innovators and their leadership will create opportunities to improve the quality of life of the RGV, Lima and beyond. If funded, this would be the first study abroad program originating from the College of Engineering and Computer Scienc e and the first extramurally funded study abroad program at UTRGV.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Training Engineers as Resilient Innovators for the RGV Region and the Nation

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
We propose the creation of the “League of Extraordinary Innovators”, an extracurricular innovation clinic to provide students with a micro-experience on technical innovation that includes problem identification, product design, product realization, and entrepreneurship.
Teams of undergraduate students from all engineering departments and levels will submit an application. Teams will be encouraged to address regional needs with their technical solutions, such as educational toys, extremely affordable prosthetics, etc. Selected teams will be coached and supported through the 2-month experience having to go through periodical reviews similar to “shark tanks” where they will receive crucial feedback. A multidisciplinary faculty group will provide advice to the teams. Students will receive a small budget and access to the Mechanical Engineering Senior Design Lab to work on their prototypes. At the end of each program (Spring and Fall), each team must present: a prototype of their product, a canvas business model, a completed Intellectual Property disclosure form, and a completed application to a national or regional design, venture or student competition. The teams will be evaluated on various metrics, for example: multidisciplinary collaboration, creativity of ideas, design effectiveness, implementation of STEM knowledge, new knowledge acquisition, social and environmental impact, etc.
Our objective is to engage the engineering student community, create a culture of innovation that instills confidence and assertiveness in our students and provides a real-life application context for STEM knowledge.
The U.S., specially our Rio Grande Valley (RGV) region requires resilient innovators capable of creating opportunities in a nascent entrepreneurial ecosystem. The non-traditional nature of the program promotes a learning environment that encourages students to take risks necessary for innovation, deal with failure and develop resiliency skills.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
UTRGV has established a leadership role promotes student success, research, creative works, health and well-being, community engagement, transnational partnerships, and sustainable development. Our student body is encouraged to take into account our society, our environment, and our economy to support UTRGV in becoming a leader in the international community for our region. He is also a professor-researcher of the School of Engineers of CETYS/Universidad, campus Ensenada. He is the Coordinator of the Environment and Sustainable Development Master’s Program of CETYS/ Universidad. His areas of research are integral coastal handling, simulation models for decision-taking, processes of public participation in environmental issues. Dr. Adeath will be discussing issues around water and sustainability.

Mr. Sanchez will be speaking to issues of space exploration and their impact on sustainability.
•	Mr. Matthew Garcia is a Senior Policy Strategist and Senior Policy Fellow in the Office of the Secretary in the Department of Energy, involved in strategic planning, analysis and program coordination as it relates to energy.  Mr. Garcia has been instrumental in working with the College of Engineering and Computer Sciences and the Office for Sustainability in supporting the new South Texas Industrial Assessment Center (STIAC) project.  Mr. Garcia will discuss how energy and sustainable development interlock and will introduce the lead team for STIAC.

These experts will attract students and faculty from the Colleges of Engineering and Computer Sciences, Office of Global Engagement, College of Sciences, and the Vackar College of Business & Entrepreneurship among others.  This opportunity provides students a pathway to becoming effective global leaders who will create a more just, inclusive society.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: NSF EEC: Establishing UTRGV's Center for Broadening Participation in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Hispanics are one of the fastest growing populations in the US, yet they are underrepresented in engineering. University X, a major Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI) with a student population over 95% Hispanic, is well-positioned to address this disparity. University X established a Center for Broadening Participation in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich (CBPE-E3) to enhance Hispanic participation in engineering from early awareness through professional employment. The CBPE -E3 aims to increase enrollment, retention, and advancement rates of Hispanic students in higher education engineering, especially Latinas facing intersectional barriers of race and gender. The CBPE -E3 envisions becoming the leading national model for inclusion, professional preparation, and successful advancement of Hispanic engineers. Drawing on the community wealth asset framework, the CBPE -E3 is grounded in culturally relevant programming and pedagogy. It encompasses three objectives and related focus areas: 1) ENGAGE (K-12 Outreach): Provide early exposure to engineering content and role models for students, their families and communities, and teachers and counselors; 2) EDUCATE (Education & Training): Create an inclusive college experience that promotes students' success through curricular reform and trainings for faculty and students; and 3) ENRICH (Professional & Research Experiences): Provide the next generation of engineers with critical professional, leadership, and research development opportunities. The CBPE -E3 builds on University X's long-standing commitment to supporting Latinx students, as recognized with a 2021 Seal of Excelencia, and in broadening participation through successful NSF ADVANCE IT, INCLUDES, and ECR grants. It also leverages partnerships with 14 entities, including major universities, engineering professional societies, community colleges, K-12 systems, non-profits, and engineering employers and alumni. The CBPE -E3 expands University X's student educational opportunities through an R1 institution collaboration to create the Alliance for Student Participation in Research Experiences for Hispanics (ASPIRE Hispanics). It also introduces students to role models, professional networks, and ongoing personal and career development through professional society partners. Finally, the CBPE -E3 shares promising practices with institutions serving largely Hispanic populations so that they can replicate or adapt best practices at their home campuses through an "Equity in Engineering Education Summit." Infrastructure in phase I will be expanded for national scale-up in phase II. The authors will present the work in progress and preliminary results from a pilot implementation. This project is funded by NSF award 2217780.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: NSF IUSE HSI Implementation and Evaluation Project: The Freshman Year Innovator Experience (FYIE): Bridging the URM Gap in STEM.
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The University of X's Freshman Year Innovator Experience (FYIE) program, hosted at a Minority Serving Institution (MSI), seeks to improve the first-year experience for new students by nurturing essential academic success skills. Specifically tailored to freshman mechanical engineering students, the program aims to equip them with self-transformation skills to navigate through the amplified academic and professional obstacles brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic. Participants of FYIE engage in two concurrent courses: Introduction to Engineering (Course A) and Learning Frameworks (Course B). In Course A, students undertake a 6-week engineering design project, while in Course B, they work on a 6-week academic career path project. Throughout these simultaneous projects, time-bound interventions highlight the similarities between the engineering design process and the academic career pathways project. The main goal is for students to recognize that the design thinking skills acquired in the engineering design process can be applied to resolve their academic career challenges. The FYIE program was initiated as a pilot in the spring semester of 2023, with instructors from Course A and B introducing the parallel projects. The implementation has continued through the fall 2023, spring 2024, and ongoing fall 2024 semesters, introducing improvements at every iteration, with adjustments made to the parallel projects and the identification of intervention points for self-transformation through analogy. The creators of the program will present the outcomes from the pilot implementations and address the obstacles and future work. INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The University of X's Freshman Year Innovator Experience (FYIE) program, hosted at a Minority Serving Institution (MSI), seeks to improve the first-year experience for new students by nurturing essential academic success skills. Specifically tailored to freshman mechanical engineering students, the program aims to equip them with self-transformation skills to navigate through the amplified academic and professional obstacles brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic. Participants of FYIE engage in two concurrent courses: Introduction to Engineering (Course A) and Learning Frameworks (Course B). In Course A, students undertake a 6-week engineering design project, while in Course B, they work on a 6-week academic career path project. Throughout these simultaneous projects, time-bound interventions highlight the similarities between the engineering design process and the academic career pathways project. The main goal is for students to recognize that the design thinking skills acquired in the engineering design process can be applied to resolve their academic career challenges. The FYIE program was initiated as a pilot in the spring semester of 2023, with instructors from Course A and B introducing the parallel projects. The implementation has continued through the fall 2023, spring 2024, and ongoing fall 2024 semesters, introducing improvements at every iteration, with adjustments made to the parallel projects and the identification of intervention points for self-transformation through analogy. The creators of the program will present the outcomes from the pilot implementations and address the obstacles and future work. This proposed endeavor is aligned with the continuous mission of the College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) at the University of X, which includes: 1) increasing the number of STEM degrees granted to Hispanics, 2) promoting the participation of women in STEM-related fields, and 3) enhancing persistence and self-confidence in STEM fields amidst the challenges posed by COVID-19. INTELLCONT.TITLE: Work in Progress: Development of A Boostcamp for Freshman Student Success During COVID-19 Transition
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Assessment results show that passing rates in introductory courses and retention rates of first-year students in the College of Engineering and Computer Science at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, a predominantly Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI), significantly dropped with the onset of COVID-19. These results and trends highlight the academic preparation of incoming students, particularly the new cohort of underrepresented Hispanic students from underserved and challenged communities in the region, who may not have sufficiently develop the necessary skills (e.g., adaptability, persistence, and performance) for the rigor of engineering education. To address this challenge, an onboarding “boostcamp” was created for incoming and transfer students to bridge the transition from secondary education to higher education. The boostcamp primes students to overcome academic deficiencies, develop a critical skills portfolio, learn problem-solving techniques, build a sustainable community of mentoring support with faculty and students, and gain a template to sustain academic and professional success during their undergraduate education. The paper presents the boostcamp's design process steps, including curricular analysis, identification of areas for improvement, skills inventory, and blueprinting, as well as its initial implementation in the mechanical engineering program. The boostcamp was organized over a week and featured hands-on engineering activities, faculty and student talks, and engineering lab tours. It was based on a design thinking approach and structured around Challenge-based Instruction, innovation, design, and mentoring. Daily activities focused on promoting critical thinking, assertiveness in the face of adversity, informed decision-making, and task prioritization. Results indicate that the boostcamp increased student confidence and established a valuable network system among participants. Future work will focus on expanding the boostcamp to include students from other engineering and computer science departments and developing a template for other institutions with similar challenges.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Work in Progress: Teaching Engineering Students to Self-Transform: Parallelisms between Product Innovation and Student Career Path Planning
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Freshman engineering students can have a hard time transitioning to college. The freshman year is critical to the students’ academic success; in this year they learn basic skills and establish essential networks with other students, faculty, and resources. How can we help these freshman engineering students in this transition? We propose that freshman students can learn from the engineering design innovation process and apply it by analogy to the design of their academic pathways. There are multiple similarities between product innovation (i.e., technology) and the continuous academic challenges faced by the student. Engineers as designers and innovators have a vast and rich repository of techniques, tools, and approaches to develop new technologies, and a parallelism can be drawn between the design and innovation of a technology (e.g., redesign of a kitchen appliance), and the “design” of the students’ academic career pathways. During the Spring 2023 semester pilot, students in Intro to Mechanical Engineering (Course A) worked in teams in a 6-week product innovation project to redesign a simple kitchen appliance. Students learned basic concepts of the design process (e.g., creative exploration of solutions, decision making, multi objective evaluation, etc.). These same students concurrently took Course B (Learning Frameworks) where they worked on a 6-week project to define their career pathways. Both projects, product innovation and career pathways, followed the Challenge Based Instruction (CBI) approach. Periodically, participant students were shown how to use the lessons from product innovation by analogy and reflection in their career pathways project. The objective is for students to learn about the engineering design process and to apply it to their academic challenges by analogy. This prepares students with meta skills to help solve future problems in their academic path, and at each iteration, the students transform themselves, hence the use of the term self-transformation (also referred as “self-innovation”). Data collected from pre and post surveys will be presented to measure self-efficacy in engineering design, grit, motivation to learn, and STEM identity. Participant interviews provide a qualitative insight into the intervention. This project is funded by NSF award 2225247.

Feasibility of Biofilters to Reduce Pollutant Emissions in Diesel Engines
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Institute of Industrial and Systems Engineers
INTELLCONT.EDITORS: H.E. Romejin, A. Schafer. R. Thomas
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Every year, heavy-duty diesel trucks (HDDV), such as commercial border trucks, idle for long periods of time waiting at the ports of entry, POE, of the United States, emitting gases such as, carbon monoxides (CO), Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs), and oxides of nitrogen (NOx).These last two are not listed within the six critical pollutants by the Environmental Protection Agency, but they serve as precursors of ozone (O3), a major pollutant which has detrimental effects on human health and the environment. Among one of the emergent control technologies in existence is biofiltration. The biofiltration process allows the removal of contaminants present in the stream of air via biochemical oxidation of organic compounds by microorganisms. In this research, a biofilter for these vehicles is designed and adopted from existing biofilters to test the removal efficiency in diesel engines. The prototype of this design will be evaluated in the capture of emissions. This paper compares existing technologies and evaluates the feasibility of using a biofilter using basic principles such as, design, cost, process, and effectiveness. Other studies have indicated a greater than 90% efficiency, but design and costs for vehicle designed biofilters are still challenges to be pursued.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Effectively Transforming Students through First Year Engineering Student Experiences
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The premise of this Research to Practice Work in Progress Paper is that promoting STEM student attraction, transfer, retention, and academic success is critical for the future workforce and the economy of our Nation especially for the underrepresented populations in the STEM workforce. At many higher education institutions, including minority serving institutions, there is a need to address primary skill deficiencies in engineering students. These deficiencies in skills can be technical and non-technical (i.e. personal, soft). Most of the current efforts from faculty and existing educational programs, focus on developing technical skills, where the faculty makes an extraordinary effort to help students learn and understand the courses' contents. For this reason, the focus of this paper is on non-technical skills for student academic success. The objectives of this paper are (1) identify the potential skills necessary to thrive in an engineering program; this includes a literature review on skills, (2) define educational experiences as interventions to develop these skills in the students, and (3); explore the metrics associated with the selected skills; this is necessary to measure improvements. These skills will enable the self-transformation of students to be more effective and successful. It is expected that a critical mass of these students will promote and nourish communities of learners. These successful students will continue their transformation into professional innovators to tackle critical needs in their respective regions. Educational experiences on innovation will help in the development of specific skills to initiate a transformation in the student that can allow them to thrive in an engineering program. This transformation of self, community (as a student), and region (as a professional) can become a model that can be transferred to other institutions interested in preparing resilient learners.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Innovation Skills for the Self-Transformation of Underrepresented Engineering Students
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Underrepresented engineering students typically face multiple challenges, for example, the lack of role models and familiar guidance during their studies. Successful students have specific characteristics (i.e. skills) that allow them to thrive. In this paper the authors explore the necessary skills that may allow students to self-transform and innovate into successful engineering students.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Development of a Multi Objective Optimization Algorithm for Biofuel Feedstock Production Considering Watershed Impacts and Land Cover Scenarios
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Weather, climate, natural climate variability and climate change could influence a number of manufacturing processes in several time and spatial scales. Specifically wood-based products are very sensitive to climatic variables like local atmospheric temperature and humidity and their changes. In the earth sciences, is a well-known fact that the long-term modes of climate variability (natural planetary low-frequency signals) can contribute and modify in a significant way the regional as well the local climatic conditions. The aim of this paper is to show a model for predicting the yearly and decadal behavior of the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) and its potential influence on the manufacturing process and final quality of wood-based musical instruments. The simulation model is based on non-linear regression analysis for the decadal part of the signal and discrete simulation for the yearly variability. The analyzed components are several elements of a polyester mix used for finished purposes that cover a wood-based guitar from a global recognized company.

INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: International Journal of Design Creativity and Innovation
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: This paper explores the 3Doodler’s, a 3D printing pen, application in the engineering design process and how it could bridge the gap between sketching and physical prototyping. We ask the research question: is the 3Doodler a better medium to communicate ideas than conventional sketching? An experiment with Engineering students aims to observe the effectiveness of the 3Doodler as a means of communicating ideas in comparison to conventional sketching. The sketch and 3Doodler groups worked on a design problem selecting modules to include on a mars rover platform. The prototypes and sketches were reviewed by interpreters to identify the intended modules. The designer’s description was compared to the final interpretation. Results indicate that 3Doodler has the potential to bridge the gap between sketching and physical prototyping, but its implementation is not trivial since it requires a proper understanding of its applicability and proper training on construction techniques.

PRESENT.ABSTRACT: According to a recent Nielsen study, ~54% of Gen Z want to be entrepreneurs. Colleges and universities have taken note and are proactively tailoring their program offerings to meet the increased demand for entrepreneurial training and education. Entrepreneurship is a powerful force that fosters innovation and creates the goods and services through which we work, play, and experience life. It is the engine that drives these mediums to be more affordable, more efficient, and more impactful, which, in theory, should lead to a better quality of life. However, if left unregulated, entrepreneurial growth can have negative consequences on certain segments of our population and the environment. Hence, a better model of innovation and entrepreneurship needs to be adopted–one that balances growth, inclusion, and sustainability and doesn’t frame them as trade-offs. Are these components mutually exclusive or can they be simultaneously prioritized? In this webinar, we’ll discuss the significance of sustainable innovation and entrepreneurship and explore the ways that growth, inclusion, and sustainability are connected through an exercise using a sustainable business model canvas.

PRESENT.NAME: 2021 VentureWell OPEN
PRESENT.TITLE: If I Can Measure It, I Can Improve It: Teaching Design & Innovation Experiences to Undergraduate Students
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Organizations (such as the d.School, KEEN, and VentureWell) have laid major groundwork in making design thinking educational resources more accessible to educators across campus and throughout the nation. As a result, engineering programs are integrating design opportunities outside of the traditional freshman introductory engineering courses and senior design capstone. Many engineering programs have developed design spines, where engineering students get to experience design throughout the typical four-year experience. Moreover, many engineering educators are starting to integrate design experiences in the mid-level fundamental courses as a way to connect theoretical concepts to real-world learning. Although design and innovation opportunities have come a long way for engineering students, there is still much to be done with respect to the development and offering of evaluation and assessment resources for engineering educators. There is a variety of approaches for evaluating and assessing design and innovation experiences, each with a different perspective. Understanding these different approaches is helpful to effectively measure the impact of design and innovation learning experiences and for continuous improvement. The purpose of this poster session is to showcase a “backwards curriculum design” holistic focused toolbox which summarizes the various learning evaluation approaches as it aligns to the learning activity and learning objective. Evaluation categories include the following: (1) Process, (2) Product/Outcome, (3) Integration of Engineering Fundamentals, (4) Constraint Focus, (5) Teamwork, and (6) Communication.

PRESENT.TITLE: Wearable Prophylaxis for the Prevention of Deep Vein Thrombosis in Patients of Post-Op Hip/ Knee Surgery
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: For patients in post-operation of hip and knee surgery, there is an increased risk of blood clots forming due to poor blood circulation. The lack of sufficient blood flow is due to reduced stimulation in the calf muscle and lack of lower leg exercise in general. Because of the possibility of blood clots forming in the deep venous systems of these patients, they are at large risk of Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and subsequently death from a Pulmonary Embolism (PE). Current solutions for DVT prevention in outpatients have many drawbacks, and a more effective and less expensive solution is desired. There is a product opportunity gap for a device which would fulfill these needs in a user-friendly and affordable manner. In this work, we propose a wearable mechanical “boot” which would aid in creating the blood flow necessary for DVT prevention. The proposed solution will increase user compliance and be a more effective means of blood flow creation while being marketable to places such as hospital purchase committees. A market study and design for manufacturability are considered in generating prototypes. The end goal is progress towards a device which will become a real product.

PRESENT.TITLE: Design and Development of an Independently Operated Aesthetic Falling Aid Device for Physically Disabled People
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: The present investigation is about a self-operated fall aid device. The main objective of this investigation was the development of a fall aid device with the functionality of being operated by the affected person without the need for external help. The secondary objective was to achieve a simple design with a low cost and capable of hiding in plain sight. The developed fall aid device provides a physically impaired person the ease of achieving a seated position after falling to the floor. The device is easily operated by solely the affected person. The apparatus includes a rigid frame divided into three sections to adapt to the human body in a seated position after the device has transformed. This structure provides a solid support to maintain the person seated. The lifting device includes a pump to inflate a set of inflatable chambers. This set of chambers is located below the middle section of the frame that act as the lifting mechanism of the apparatus. As previously mentioned, one of the main features of the device is its simple design and ability to be hidden in plain sight. This was done by disguising it as a rug that can be placed anywhere in a room. The method used to develop this investigation was the observation of similar product to achieve the objective of helping a disabled person to be lifted from the ground.
